headline: Bishkek bars flat sales before walls stand; Talas complex's prices stay unpublished
dek: Kyrgyzstan acted after more than 40 builders left buyers without flats; in western Talas, a 495-flat complex due in 2027 has published neither its prices nor its lenders.
paragraphs: Kyrgyzstan has barred construction companies from selling flats while a site is still at the excavation or foundation stage. Units may now be sold only once the building's structure stands. Bishkek gave as its reason the more than 40 companies that have left buyers without the flats they paid for. The rule applies in Kyrgyzstan alone. Nothing changes in Irad, but the question it raises is a Talas one: what can a buyer see before handing over money?

IradOne reported the Kyrgyz step on Friday. The Herald looked at what Talas buyers can actually check, and found that the answer for the city's largest current project is: very little that is published.

Talas Turak-Jay Kurulush LLC is building a 495-flat mortgage complex on city land in western Talas: eleven nine-storey blocks, about 45 flats a block, due in 2027. A billboard at the Trans-Talas Highway sells it as Alma-Bak. Prices and lenders have not been published. The Herald asked the company on Friday for a price list, the names of the banks taking part and the stage the foundations have reached. It had not replied by deadline.

Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, said the Kyrgyz rule targets one specific risk. 'Whoever pays before the walls stand is lending to the builder, and a buyer is the worst-placed lender in the chain,' she said. 'He has no collateral and no say in how the money is spent.' She said a buyer in Talas could reasonably ask to see the company's title to the land, the permit for the block he is buying into, the name of any bank financing the project and the state of the company's earlier buildings. 'None of that is rude to ask. If a seller will not answer, that is also information.'

Prof. Akmatova added that payment in dollars sharpens the risk. The official rate is 8.40 som to the dollar, while the Bazar-i Kalan changers sold dollars at 11.95 this morning. A family saving in som, or one waiting on a relative's transfer, can see the price of a flat move before the first instalment is due. A one-room flat rents for 1,000–1,500 som a month in Talas, and landlords in the new towers ask in dollars. Families who buy are often choosing between a rent that follows the dollar and a purchase made in dollars.

The nearest local picture is not a failed firm but the Etek plots. The city allotted them from 2009 to teachers, doctors, gendarmes and Defense Corps officers. Many of the large two-storey brick houses there stand unfinished, built a floor at a time as money arrives, much of it from relatives in the United States and Russia. Prof. Akmatova said self-builders carry their own risk, but they can see every course of brick they pay for. A flat buyer cannot.

Gulmira Sadykova, 69, a retired school canteen cook in the Köhne Diz, said she would not pay anyone for a flat she could not walk into. 'I have seen what a promise costs when the cement runs out,' she said. 'Keep your som under the mattress until there is a door to open.' She was speaking in general; she is not a buyer in any current project.

The Herald found no published Talas rule on what a developer must show a buyer, and the card of facts for this story does not suggest one is planned. The company's reply, once received, will be published. Whether the 2027 date holds will be visible from the street long before it appears in a sale contract.
